raw_case_text:
A 32-years-old woman without significant past medical history was hospitalized in our department with 15 days history of shortness of breath. Physical examination was unremarkable, and the patient denied any exposure to asbestos. Electrocardiogram (ECG) showed sinus rhythm. There were no conduction or repolarization abnormalities. Chest X-ray showed an enlarged heart (Figure 1). Transthoracic echocardiography (TEE) revealed a mild pericardial effusion without signs of cardiac tamponade and with preserved biventricular function. The diagnosis of acute pericarditis was retained, and the patient was discharged in a stable condition with colchicine and ibuprofen.
A month later, she was readmitted for chest pain. On physical examination, she has not been febrile and there were no heart murmur or signs of pulmonary congestion. Her central venous pressure was normal and there was no pedal edema. Vital signs showed a blood pressure of 96/55 mmHg, a pulse of 110 beats per minute, and peripheral oxygen saturation of 98%. ECG revealed sinus rhythm tachycardia with negative T waves in inferior and antero-septo-apical leads (Figure 2). TEE showed a worsening of the pericardial effusion but with no signs of right ventricular chambers collapse. We further noted an incipient systolic right ventricular dysfunction. Creatinin, troponin and NT pro-BNP levels were within normal ranges. Hepatic and thyroid functions were normal. Inflammatory markers were elevated with a c reactive protein level of 166 mg/L. Blood count revealed anemia. Cardiac tomography (CT) scan showed a circumferential pericardial effusion with no pericardial thickening or other abnormalities (Figure 3).
Auto-immune pericarditis was unlikely as we did not detect positive rheumatoid factor, cryoglobilins, antinuclear, and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies. Further investigations including serology for viruses commonly incriminated in pericarditis, human immunodeficiency virus, brucellosis, salmonellosis, toxoplasmosis, fever Q and Lyme disease as well as tuberculin skin test were also negative. Thus, a definitive diagnosis could not be obtained, so we opted for pericardiocentesis. Cytological examination showed subacute inflammation with lympho-plasmacytic predominance and mesothelial hyperplasia, but without any signs of malignancy. The patient was treated for suspected tuberculous pericarditis. Six weeks later, with the decrease in corticosteroid therapy, she consulted for recurrence of the same symptomatology. TEE was performed and showed a pericardial effusion with paradoxical septal motion (Figure 4). She was scheduled then for a thoracoscopic surgical biopsy. Histopathological examination of the specimen confirmed the diagnosis of malignant mesothelioma with right ventricular myocardial invasion. On immuno-histo-chemistry, neoplastic cells were strongly positive for calcretinin and WT1 protein. We referred her for palliative chemo and radiotherapy, but she died of refractory heart failure 4 months following the definitive diagnosis.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 32-year-old woman presented with a 15-day history of shortness of breath, followed 1 month later by readmission for acute chest pain and recurrent pericardial effusion.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 32-year-old woman was initially hospitalized for 15 days of dyspnea and diagnosed with acute pericarditis (mild pericardial effusion on TTE), for which she was discharged on colchicine and ibuprofen. She was readmitted 1 month later with chest pain and worsening pericardial effusion, and recurred again 6 weeks after empiric antituberculous and corticosteroid therapy with constrictive/tamponade physiology.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unremarkable past medical history; denied occupational or environmental asbestos exposure.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for dyspnea and recurrent chest pain; negative for fever.

objective.physical_examination: Initial admission: unremarkable exam. Readmission 1 month later: afebrile, blood pressure 96/55 mmHg, heart rate 110 beats/min, SpO2 98%, normal central venous pressure, no cardiac murmur, pulmonary congestion, or pedal edema.
objective.routine_investigations: Anemia and markedly elevated CRP (166 mg/L); normal creatinine, troponin, NT-proBNP, hepatic, and thyroid function tests. Negative RF, cryoglobulins, viral pericarditis serologies, HIV, brucellosis, salmonellosis, toxoplasmosis, Q fever, Lyme disease, and tuberculin skin test. Initial ECG showed normal sinus rhythm; readmission ECG showed sinus tachycardia with inferior and anteroseptoapical T-wave inversions. Chest X-ray showed cardiomegaly. Serial TTEs showed progression from a mild pericardial effusion to a large circumferential effusion with incipient right ventricular systolic dysfunction and subsequent paradoxical interventricular septal motion.
objective.advanced_workup: ANA and ANCA negative. Chest CT demonstrated a circumferential pericardial effusion without pericardial thickening or pulmonary masses. Pericardiocentesis fluid cytology showed lymphoplasmacytic inflammation and mesothelial hyperplasia without malignant cells. Thoracoscopic surgical pericardial biopsy histopathology and immunohistochemistry (strongly positive for calretinin and WT1) confirmed primary malignant pericardial mesothelioma invading the right ventricular myocardium.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Thoracoscopic pericardial biopsy histopathology and calretinin/WT1 immunohistochemistry (following negative infectious/Brucella, autoimmune, and tuberculosis workups and failure of colchicine/ibuprofen and empiric antituberculous/steroid therapy) confirmed primary malignant pericardial mesothelioma with right ventricular myocardial invasion. Referred for palliative chemotherapy and radiotherapy, but died of refractory heart failure 4 months after diagnosis.
